title: Why do leaves change colors in the fall?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss why leaves change color in the fall. They open with a mustache-growing fundraiser plug and banter about a "Rush Fan" license plate and a drug artist. They cover leaf peeping locations (Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, the Smokies, Appalachians, the West), and a Shoshoni legend about the Great Bear's blood and fat coloring the leaves. The science section explains chlorophyll and photosynthesis, how carotenoids and xanthophylls show yellow and orange once chlorophyll breaks down, the cork-like abscission layer that seals the leaf off, and anthocyanins that produce reds, with the theory that dry summers and warm sunny days followed by cool nights favor red. They mention the leaf peeper app and a listener mail about Sherpas and Sir Edmund Hillary's Everest photo, followed by a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and mustache fundraiser
segments.summary: Josh plugs his November mustache fundraiser for prostate cancer research. The hosts banter about a Rush fan license plate and an internet artist who drew self-portraits under drugs.

segments.title: Fall foliage and leaf peeping
segments.summary: The hosts discuss autumn as a favorite season, the heavily wooded Georgia, and the term leaf peeping. They list leaf-viewing regions including New England, the Southeast, the Appalachians, and the West.

segments.title: Shoshoni legend of the Great Bear
segments.summary: The hosts relate the Shoshoni legend that the Great Bear's blood turned leaves red and its fat splashing from a pot turned them yellow. Josh notes that science has better explanations.
topics: Native American folklore about leaf color

segments.title: Photosynthesis and chlorophyll
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain that chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, and that photosynthesis turns light into chemical energy and then glucose. As days shorten, the plant stops making chlorophyll.

segments.title: Yellow and orange pigments and the abscission layer
segments.summary: Carotenoids and xanthophylls, which give carrots and eggs their color, show yellow and orange once chlorophyll is gone. The tree forms a cork-like separation layer at the leaf base that seals the leaf off.

segments.title: Anthocyanins and red leaves
segments.summary: Anthocyanins, flavonoid pigments that produce reds and purples, are made in the leaf as the tree tries to recover sugar. Dry summers and warm sunny days followed by cool nights favor brilliant red displays. Japanese maple and sugar maple are mentioned.

segments.title: Leaf peeper app and wrap-up of science
segments.summary: The hosts summarize that science is sure about yellow and green but less certain about red. They mention a free Leaf Peeper app with a color-coded US map of leaf change stages.

segments.title: Listener mail about Sherpas and Sir Edmund Hillary
segments.summary: A listener shares a story about his uncle, a New Zealand photographer who took a photo of Edmund Hillary training and later mailed copies to newspapers after the Everest ascent. The hosts also mention the back catalog and invite listeners to share fall photos.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to share photos of hometown fall trees and to contact the show on Twitter, Facebook, or email, then close the episode.
